Part B · Chapter B4

Backpropagation

How backpropagation computes the slope of the loss for all weights of a network in one backward pass

Gradient descent needs the slope of the loss for a weight. Backpropagation computes these slopes in one backward pass, using the chain rule node by node. This chapter runs it by hand on a tiny network, checks the slopes with finite differences and shows why long chains of small slopes can leave early layers barely learning.

The sharks are made up: records generated from published length-weight relationships, not field data.

You will need: the chain rule (0.6), graphs and DAGs (0.4), the outer product (0.5), a neuron with an activation (B1) and a loss with gradient descent (B3).

The network as a graph

Guess first. The network in the figure takes the scaled length and girth of Tag 3305, an adult spadenose shark, with made-up starting values for its nine weights and biases. Will the network give this shark a chance of being adult above 50% or below 50%?

The figure is a computation graph, a diagram of nodes (numbers) joined by arrows. A node is an input, a weight, or a value computed by one simple step from the nodes that point to it. The forward pass computes the nodes from the inputs to the loss \(L\), and it computes a node only after the nodes it uses. Here \(p\) is the network's chance that the shark is an adult, and \(L\) is large when \(p\) is far from the label \(y\) (\(y = 1\) means adult).

  1. Press Step: a click fills one dashed box, and the equation boxes under the graph show how its value was computed.
  2. Press Forward to fill the rest: the readout under the graph ends at a chance of adult \(p\) = 0.342 and a loss \(L\) = 1.073.
  3. Click the box \(c\), drag Value to 0 and press Forward again: \(p\) rises to 0.561 and \(L\) falls to 0.578.

The starting weights give Tag 3305 a 34.2% chance of being adult, so the loss is 1.073.

How it works

Take Tag 3305, with scaled length \(x_1 = 0.22\) and girth \(x_2 = 0.21\). A hidden unit is a neuron between the inputs and the output. It adds its inputs times weights and a bias to give a score \(z\), and its value is the activation \(h = \tanh z = (e^{z}-e^{-z})/(e^{z}+e^{-z})\) of that score. Hidden unit 1 gives \(z_1 = w_{11}x_1 + w_{12}x_2 + b_1 = 0.8\times0.22 + (-0.6)\times0.21 + 0.1 = 0.150\) and \(h_1 = \tanh 0.150 = 0.149\) (a calculator, or the boxes under the graph, gives the values of tanh, the exponential \(e^x\) and the logarithm \(\ln\)). Hidden unit 2 has other weights, so \(z_2 = w_{21}x_1 + w_{22}x_2 + b_2 = (-0.4)\times0.22 + 0.7\times0.21 + (-0.2) = -0.141\) and \(h_2 = \tanh(-0.141) = -0.140\).

zooutput score=0.134v1 h1 = 0.9 × 0.149+0.112v2 h2 = −0.8 × −0.140+−0.9c=−0.654its value→ σ →0.342p→ −ln →1.073loss, y = 1

The output weights \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) multiply the hidden values, \(c\) is the output bias, and the sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})\) turns the score \(z_o\) into the chance \(p = 1/(1+e^{0.654}) = 0.342\). For the label \(y = 1\) the log loss is \(L = -\ln p = 1.073\), and for \(y = 0\) it is \(-\ln(1-p)\). Here the hidden units add 0.246 and the bias subtracts 0.9, so the score is negative. A score of 0 gives \(\sigma(0) = 0.5\) and a negative score gives less, so \(p\) is below 50%, which answers the guess. The shark is an adult, so the network starts out wrong about it.

Analogy. The graph is a spreadsheet: a cell is a formula of the cells before it, and you fill the cells in from the top.

Where it breaks. In a spreadsheet you type the numbers and leave them alone. In a network, training changes the weights, so training needs the slope of the last cell, the loss, with respect to the weights. A spreadsheet has no step that runs backward; the next section adds one.

Quick quiz

In what order must the nodes be computed, and why?

Any order in which a node comes after all the nodes it uses, because a node's value is computed from theirs. In this graph that means the inputs, then the hidden sums and activations, then the output score, then \(p\), then the loss.

Switch the label to y = 0 and press Forward. Why does the loss go down?

With \(y = 0\) the network's 34.2% chance of adult is nearer the label than it was for \(y = 1\). The loss becomes \(-\ln(1-p) = -\ln 0.658 = 0.42\), against 1.073 before.

The inputs and the label

Click an input or a weight to select it, then change it with the slider and run the network again. The two inputs are the length (41.0 cm) and girth (11.5 cm) of Tag 3305. They are standardised with the spadenose mean and spread from A3 (0.7), so they read 0.22 and 0.21 spreads above the average. The label \(y = 1\) means adult.

The same steps in symbols

A node needs only the nodes before it. The backward pass of the next section uses that order in reverse. The same steps in symbols:

\[ \mathbf{z}^{[1]} = W^{[1]}\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}^{[1]},\qquad \mathbf{h} = g(\mathbf{z}^{[1]}),\qquad z_o = \mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{h} + c,\qquad p = \sigma(z_o) \]

\[ \ell = -y\ln p - (1-y)\ln(1-p) \]

  • \(\mathbf{x}\) is the list of two scaled inputs, and \(W^{[1]}\) is the 2 by 2 matrix of first-layer weights \(w_{ji}\) (row \(j\) is a hidden unit, column \(i\) an input). \(\mathbf{b}^{[1]}\) is the list of biases \(b_1, b_2\).
  • \(g\) is the hidden activation (tanh to start with) and \(\mathbf{h}\) the two hidden values \(h_1, h_2\).
  • \(\mathbf{v}\) is the row of two output weights \(v_1, v_2\) (the matrix \(W^{[2]}\)), \(c\) the output bias (\(\mathbf{b}^{[2]}\)) and \(z_o\) the output score.
  • \(\sigma(z_o)\) is the sigmoid of the score. \(\ell\) is the log loss of this one shark, the loss \(L\) of the figure; for a batch, \(L\) is the average of the \(\ell\) values (B3).

Hidden unit 2 with its parts labelled

The boxes below repeat the arithmetic of hidden unit 2 for Tag 3305. The sum node adds two products and the bias, then tanh maps the result into the range from −1 to 1.

−0.4w21×0.22x1+0.7w22×0.21x2+−0.2b2=−0.141z2→ tanh →−0.140h2

A second shark

Now a second shark, to see the same graph give a different answer. Tag 4127 is a juvenile grey bamboo shark, so its label is \(y = 0\). Standardised with the spadenose numbers (44.0 cm and 12.4 cm) it reads 0.56 and 0.57. That scaling is only a convenient way to feed the network a second input, because a bamboo shark has its own average and spread. The forward pass gives \(z_1 = 0.208\), \(z_2 = -0.025\), \(h = (0.205, -0.025)\), \(z_o = -0.696\) and \(p = 0.333\). For \(y = 0\) the loss is \(-\ln(1 - 0.333) = 0.405\). The network happens to be right about this shark, so its loss is small.

The code below runs both sharks through the same function. Only the input and the label change. That is why a framework can send a whole batch through the graph in a single pass.

import numpy as np

W1 = np.array([[0.8, -0.6], [-0.4, 0.7]]); b1 = np.array([0.1, -0.2])
W2 = np.array([0.9, -0.8]);                 b2 = -0.9

def forward(x, y):
    z1 = W1 @ x + b1;  h = np.tanh(z1)                 # hidden sums, then tanh
    zo = W2 @ h + b2;  p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-zo))       # output score, then chance of adult
    loss = -np.log(p) if y == 1 else -np.log(1 - p)    # log loss of this one shark
    return z1, h, zo, p, loss

for name, x, y in [("Tag 3305", [0.22, 0.21], 1), ("Tag 4127", [0.5644, 0.5731], 0)]:
    z1, h, zo, p, loss = forward(np.array(x), y)
    print(name, "z1 =", z1.round(3), "h =", h.round(3), "z_o =", round(zo, 3), "p =", round(p, 4), "loss =", round(loss, 4))
Tag 3305 z1 = [ 0.15  -0.141] h = [ 0.149 -0.14 ] z_o = -0.654 p = 0.3421 loss = 1.0726
Tag 4127 z1 = [ 0.208 -0.025] h = [ 0.205 -0.025] z_o = -0.696 p = 0.3327 loss = 0.4045

What counts as a node

A step is one operation whose local slope (defined in the next section) is known and cheap to compute: a sum, a product, tanh, a sigmoid, a logarithm. A node of the graph is the result of one step. A framework ships a library of such operations (PyTorch lists over a thousand operators) and builds all models from them. PyTorch records the graph while the forward pass runs, so a different input can run a different graph. In this figure a node contains one number, and a working network has millions of numbers. A framework usually groups them into arrays, so one node of its graph can be the result of a whole array operation such as a matrix product (see “Whole layers at once” below). Seen number by number, the picture is the one above with many more circles.

Why any order that respects the arrows works

Why can we run the nodes in any order that respects the arrows? Because the graph has no loops (a DAG, 0.4), so a node never waits on itself. If a graph had a loop, one pass would not be enough to fill it. This chapter's graphs have none.

In practice: check the first loss

A network that starts with small random weights has scores near 0, so it gives \(p\) near 0.5 and a loss near \(\ln 2 \approx 0.69\) for a yes-or-no label. Here the first loss is 1.07 because the made-up output bias is \(-0.9\). When you build your own network, compute the loss on the first batch before any training. If it is far from 0.69, check the inputs, the labels and the output layer first (B8). Keep inputs near 0 with a spread of about 1, as in A2. Large inputs push tanh into its flat tails from the first step.

More questions

Set the output bias \(c\) to 0 and run Forward on Tag 3305. Is the chance of being adult now above or below 50%, and why?

Above. The score becomes \(0.134 + 0.112 = 0.246\), so \(p = \sigma(0.246) = 0.561\) and the loss falls to \(-\ln 0.561 = 0.578\). The bias of \(-0.9\) was what kept the first answer below 50%.

Sending the slopes back

Guess first. The slope of the loss with respect to a weight says how fast the loss changes when the weight goes up by a small amount. Which weight or bias has the slope of largest size (absolute value) at the starting values? Choose among an output weight (\(v_1\) or \(v_2\)), the output bias \(c\) and a first-layer weight such as \(w_{11}\).

Backpropagation is a forward pass followed by a backward pass from the loss to the inputs. At a node, the upstream slope is the slope of the loss with respect to that node, which the nodes closer to the loss have already passed back. A local slope is the slope of the node's value with respect to one of its inputs. By the chain rule their product is the slope of the loss with respect to that input through this node. One backward pass can then give the slopes of all nine weights and biases.

  1. Press Backward. Coral slopes fill in on the nodes and weights, and the boxes below the graph show an upstream slope (coral) times a local slope (navy) for the latest step.
  2. Press Update: all nine numbers move against their slopes (learning rate \(\eta = 0.3\)) and the loss goes from 1.073 to 0.771.

At the starting values the slope of largest size belongs to the output bias \(c\) (−0.658), and its negative sign means that raising \(c\) lowers the loss.

How it works

For Tag 3305, the upstream slope at the output score \(z_o\) is \(p - y = 0.342 - 1 = -0.658\) (the Go deeper section derives it). Nudging an input of a sum node changes the sum by the same amount, so the local slope is 1. The bias \(c\) is added to \(z_o\), so its slope is \(-0.658\). Nudging a factor of a product node changes the product by the nudge times the other factor, so the local slope is the other factor. The node \(h_1\) is multiplied by \(v_1 = 0.9\), so its slope is \(-0.658 \times 0.9 = -0.592\). Other weights and biases get the arriving slope times factors below 1 in size, so \(c\) has the largest slope.

−0.658upstream slope ∂L/∂zo×0.900local slope ∂zo/∂h1 = v1=−0.592slope of h1

A local slope uses only forward values; for tanh it is \(1 - h^2\) (the slope rules). A node or weight \(a\) used by the nodes \(b_k\) has the slope \(\partial L/\partial a = \sum_k (\partial L/\partial b_k)(\partial b_k/\partial a)\). Here \(\partial L/\partial a\) is the slope of \(L\) with respect to \(a\), and \(\sum_k\) adds the terms (upstream times local) of the nodes that use \(a\). The Update button moves a weight \(w\) to \(w - \eta\,\partial L/\partial w\), where \(\eta\) is the learning rate.

Common belief. Backpropagation is the way a network learns.

Why it fails. Backpropagation only computes slopes: after Backward no weight has changed, and learning happens when something uses the slopes to move the weights.

Better account. Backpropagation answers “which way and how steeply”. An optimiser is a rule that turns slopes into weight updates. Gradient descent, the rule of this section, chooses only how far to move, while momentum and Adam, in the next chapter, also change the direction.

Quick quiz

The slope arriving at the output score is −0.658. The weight \(v_1\) multiplies \(h_1 = 0.149\). What is the slope of \(v_1\)?

\(-0.658 \times 0.149 = -0.098\). The product node sends the slope times the other factor, and the other factor of \(v_1\) is \(h_1\).

Why does the backward pass need the values from the forward pass?

Local slopes depend on them. The local slope for \(v_1\) is \(h_1\), the slope of tanh is \(1-h^2\), and the slope of the sigmoid is \(p(1-p)\). The forward pass has to keep those values until the backward pass uses them.

Go deeper derivation of p − y, a second shark, code about 7 min

Reading the figure

Look at steps 8 and 11 of the backward pass. The input \(x_1\) feeds both hidden units, so it gets one slope from either of two paths, and the two add. The next section explains that sum.

After an Update the network is rerun, and the new loss appears in the history plot. Three more presses lower the loss from 0.771 to 0.569, 0.435 and 0.343. The loss falls quickly at first and then more slowly, as in A2.

All nine slopes at the starting values

A bias has the shortest route to the loss, and a weight multiplies the arriving slope by the value it reads. All the values on the way are below 1 here: the hidden values are 0.149 and \(-0.140\), and the inputs 0.22 and 0.21. The three biases have the slopes \(-0.658\), \(-0.579\) and \(+0.516\), and the slopes of the first-layer weights and the output weights are 0.11 to 0.13 and 0.09 to 0.10 in size. The slope of a weight scales with the value in front of it, which is one reason inputs are standardised (A2).

Why the slope at the score is p − y

The simplification in step 2 is the slope that A3 derived for log loss, and it takes a few short lines. First, the sigmoid's own slope. Write \(\sigma(z) = (1 + e^{-z})^{-1}\). The chain rule gives \(\sigma'(z) = e^{-z}(1+e^{-z})^{-2}\). Split the fraction as \(\tfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}\cdot\tfrac{e^{-z}}{1+e^{-z}}\), and the second factor equals \(1 - \sigma(z)\). So \(\sigma' = \sigma(1-\sigma)\), which is the number \(p(1-p) = 0.225\) in the figure. Then multiply by the slope of the log loss:

\[ \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial z_o} = \Big(-\frac{y}{p} + \frac{1-y}{1-p}\Big)\,p(1-p) = -y(1-p) + (1-y)\,p = p - y \]

  • The bracket is \(\partial\ell/\partial p\), the slope of the log loss. The second factor is the sigmoid's slope.
  • Multiplying out, the terms \(-yp\) and \(+yp\) cancel, which leaves \(p - y\). For \(y = 1\) it is \(p - 1\), always negative, so the score is always pushed up.

A second shark

Now a second shark through the same steps. Tag 4127 (label \(y = 0\), \(p = 0.333\), inputs 0.564 and 0.573 before rounding) gives \(\partial\ell/\partial z_o = p - y = +0.333\), a positive slope, so the update will lower the score. Going back, \(\partial\ell/\partial h = 0.333 \times (0.9, -0.8) = (0.299, -0.266)\). Times the tanh slopes \((0.958, 0.999)\) this gives \(\partial\ell/\partial z = (0.287, -0.266)\). The weight \(w_{11}\) finally gets its slope:

0.287upstream ∂L/∂z1×0.564local: input x1=0.162∂L/∂w11 for Tag 4127

The sign is the opposite of the \(w_{11}\) slope for Tag 3305 (\(-0.127\)). A juvenile label gives a slope that lowers the score at the next update, and an adult label gives one that raises it. With many sharks in a batch, the slopes of all of them are averaged (B3).

Why it works, and where it stops

The chain rule is a statement about small nudges. A local slope describes a node near its current value, and the product tells you what a small nudge of a weight does to the loss. It breaks where a node has no usable slope. ReLU has a corner at 0 (libraries usually use a slope of 0 there). Rounding, a hard threshold or an argmax has a slope of 0 at nearly all points, so no slope reaches the weights behind it. That is one reason the step activation gave way to smooth ones (B1).

Cost in practice

The backward pass needs the forward values, so a framework stores them. Memory grows with the number of nodes and with the batch size, and the backward pass costs a small multiple of the forward pass. The Update button's \(\eta\) goes up to 2. In this figure the loss falls at any \(\eta\) the slider allows, but by less than the slope predicts (0.746 against 1.108 at \(\eta = 1\)).

An update by hand, and the size of the drop

Take \(\eta = 0.3\). The output bias moves from \(-0.9\) to \(-0.9 - 0.3\times(-0.658) = -0.703\). The weight \(v_1\) moves from 0.9 to \(0.9 - 0.3\times(-0.098) = 0.929\), and \(w_{11}\) from 0.8 to 0.838. All nine numbers move together, against their own slopes.

Does the loss fall by the amount the slopes promise? For a small step, a weight that moves by \(-\eta g\) changes the loss by about \(g\times(-\eta g)\). Adding up all nine weights and biases gives a change of \(-\eta\sum g^2\). This is negative unless all the slopes are 0, so a small enough step lowers the loss.

predicted drop0.3η×1.108sum of the nine squared slopes=0.332predicted drop|1.073 − 0.771loss before and after=0.302actual drop

The prediction is close for small steps and drifts for large ones. At \(\eta = 0.05\) it says 0.0554 and the loss drops by 0.0546. At \(\eta = 1\) it says 1.108 and the loss drops by only 0.746, because the loss curves away from the straight line that the slope describes. The code checks these three steps and then runs five updates in a row.

import numpy as np

x = np.array([0.22, 0.21]); y = 1.0
theta = np.array([0.8, -0.6, -0.4, 0.7, 0.1, -0.2, 0.9, -0.8, -0.9])   # W1 (4), b1 (2), W2 (2), b2

def loss_and_grad(t):
    W1, b1, W2, b2 = t[:4].reshape(2, 2), t[4:6], t[6:8], t[8]
    h = np.tanh(W1 @ x + b1)
    p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(W2 @ h + b2)))
    d2 = p - y                                  # slope at the output score
    d1 = d2 * W2 * (1 - h ** 2)                 # slope at the hidden sums
    return -np.log(p), np.concatenate([np.outer(d1, x).ravel(), d1, d2 * h, [d2]])

loss, g = loss_and_grad(theta)
print("sum of squared slopes =", round((g ** 2).sum(), 3))
for eta in (0.05, 0.3, 1.0):
    new_loss, _ = loss_and_grad(theta - eta * g)
    print(f"eta {eta}: predicted drop {eta * (g ** 2).sum():.4f}, actual drop {loss - new_loss:.4f}")

for step in range(5):                           # five updates in a row, eta = 0.3
    loss, g = loss_and_grad(theta)
    print("update", step, " loss =", round(loss, 4))
    theta = theta - 0.3 * g
sum of squared slopes = 1.108
eta 0.05: predicted drop 0.0554, actual drop 0.0546
eta 0.3: predicted drop 0.3324, actual drop 0.3018
eta 1.0: predicted drop 1.1080, actual drop 0.7464
update 0  loss = 1.0726
update 1  loss = 0.7708
update 2  loss = 0.569
update 3  loss = 0.4346
update 4  loss = 0.3435

Try it: a ReLU unit that gives 0

Switch the activation to ReLU, press Forward, then Backward. One hidden unit has a negative sum and gives 0. What happens to the slopes of its weights and bias?

Answer

They are all 0. The ReLU slope is 0 for a negative score, so the product at that step is 0 and no slope flows back to \(w_{21}\), \(w_{22}\) or \(b_2\). A unit stuck like this learns no more until something else moves its score (B8 shows how to spot dead units).

Symbols

\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial a} \;=\; \sum_{k}\frac{\partial L}{\partial b_k}\,\frac{\partial b_k}{\partial a} \qquad\qquad w \;\leftarrow\; w - \eta\,\frac{\partial L}{\partial w} \]

  • \(a\) is any node or weight, and \(b_k\) are the nodes that use \(a\) as an input. If only one node uses \(a\), the sum has one term.
  • \(\partial L/\partial b_k\) is the upstream slope from node \(b_k\), and \(\partial b_k/\partial a\) is the local slope of that one step.
  • The right-hand rule is the gradient step of A2: \(\eta\) is the learning rate and the arrow means "replace".

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If the loss goes up after an Update, the step size \(\eta\) is probably too large for the curvature (0.6). Halve it and try again. If the loss rises whatever \(\eta\) is, suspect a wrong sign or a wrong local slope in the backward code, and run the gradient check at the end of this chapter.

A common mistake in PyTorch is calling loss.backward() again without clearing the stored slopes first. The new slopes are added to the old ones, so the step uses a sum of old and new slopes, which makes it too big and partly stale (B8 lists the other usual suspects).

Where this is used

Used in: the optimisers of B5 take these slopes as input. The slope of the loss with respect to an input (the \(\partial L/\partial x_1\) box) is the raw material of the saliency maps in B9.

More questions

Which nodes in the graph receive a slope from two paths?

The inputs \(x_1\) and \(x_2\), because both of them feed both hidden units. The weights, the hidden values and the output nodes feed a single later node apiece.

A value used twice

Guess first. In the figure the value \(x = 3\) is used by two nodes, \(p = 2x\) and \(q = x^2\), and the node \(y = p \times q\) uses both. If you nudge \(x\) up by 0.01, does \(y\) rise by about 0.18, 0.36 or 0.54?

A path is a route along arrows from a node to the output \(y\). The slope along a path is the product of the local slopes on it. A node used by several later nodes has several paths. The slope of \(y\) with respect to that node is the sum of the slopes along all of them. In backpropagation the slope that arrives from a new path is added to the total so far.

  1. Choose Path through \(p\), then Path through \(q\): the boxes show the slope along one path alone, 18.0 and then 36.0, which is only part of the total.
  2. Choose Both paths: the boxes add to 54.0, and the nudge test \((y(x+0.01) - y(x)) \div 0.01\) gives 54.18, so a nudge of 0.01 raises \(y\) by about 0.54.
  3. Drag \(x\) to \(-2\): the paths are 8.0 and 16.0, they add to 24.0, and the nudge test gives 23.88. Set \(x\) back to 3.

At \(x = 3\) the two paths give 18 and 36, which add to 54, so a nudge of 0.01 raises \(y\) by about 0.54.

How it works

Take \(x = 3\). Then \(p = 2x = 6\) and \(q = x^2 = 9\). Write \(dx\) for a small nudge of \(x\), and \(dp\), \(dq\) and \(dy\) for the changes it causes in \(p\), \(q\) and \(y = pq\). Since \(p = 2x\) and \(q = x^2\), \(dp = 2\,dx\) and \(dq = 2x\,dx\) (the slope rules). A product changes by about \(dy = q\,dp + p\,dq\), because both factors change, and dividing by \(dx\) gives \(dy/dx = q\cdot 2 + p\cdot 2x = 9\cdot 2 + 6\cdot 6 = 54\).

∂y/∂x = 54the slope of y with respect to x=9 × 2 = 18path through p: q × dp/dx+6 × 6 = 36path through q: p × dq/dx

The paths add because a nudge of \(x\) reaches \(y\) along both of them, and for a small nudge the two changes of \(y\) add. This is the formula of the last section: the slope of a node is a sum over the nodes that use it. A weight used at several places is also a node that several nodes use, so its slope is the sum over those places. A filter of a convolutional network is an example, since it reads many positions.

Common belief. A value that is used twice gets the average of the slopes along its two paths.

Why it fails. A nudge of \(x\) travels along both paths, so \(y\) feels both effects. The average of 18 and 36 is 27, and the true slope is 54.

Better account. Add the paths. An average does come later, over the examples of a batch.

Quick quiz

A node \(u\) is used twice: \(s = u\,v + u\). The slope arriving at \(s\) is 5, with \(u = 2\) and \(v = 3\). What slope reaches \(u\)?

Two paths. Through the product: \(5 \times v = 15\). Through the plain \(+u\): \(5 \times 1 = 5\). Total 20.

A weight is used at four places, and the slopes it receives from them are \(-0.1\), \(0.3\), \(0.2\) and \(-0.2\). What is the slope of the weight, and why is the average wrong?

The four contributions add to \(0.2\). The average would be 0.05. A nudge of the weight changes all four uses, so the loss feels the sum.

Terms

One node feeding several later nodes is called a fan-out. Adding the slope from a new path to the total so far is called accumulating.

The formula in symbols

\[ \frac{dy}{dx} = \underbrace{q\,\frac{dp}{dx}}_{\text{path through }p} + \underbrace{p\,\frac{dq}{dx}}_{\text{path through }q} = 9\cdot 2 + 6\cdot 6 = 54 \]

  • \(x\) is the value used twice. \(p = 2x\) and \(q = x^2\) are the two nodes that use it, and \(y = pq\) is the node that uses both.
  • At \(x = 3\): \(p = 6\), \(q = 9\), \(dp/dx = 2\) and \(dq/dx = 2x = 6\). A path contributes its local slope times the other factor, and the paths add. The total 54 agrees with \(6x^2\), the slope of \(y = 2x^3\), at \(x = 3\).

Why the nudge test gives 54.18

The nudge estimate 54.18 differs a little from 54 because the nudge is finite and the curve bends. The slopes of this section describe the curve at one point, in the limit of a small nudge, and only approximate it for a finite nudge.

In code

In code the sum is one line. The last number is the nudge test from the figure.

x = 3.0
p, q = 2 * x, x ** 2            # two nodes use x
y = p * q                       # and one node uses both
dy_dp, dy_dq = q, p             # a product sends the slope times the other factor
dx = dy_dp * 2 + dy_dq * 2 * x  # two paths into x: add them
nudge = (2 * (x + 0.01) * (x + 0.01) ** 2 - y) / 0.01
print("paths:", dy_dp * 2, "+", dy_dq * 2 * x, "=", dx, "  nudge test:", round(nudge, 2))
paths: 18.0 + 36.0 = 54.0   nudge test: 54.18

Why add, and how many paths there are

Adding is right because a small nudge acts in a straight line. To first order, the effect through \(p\) and the effect through \(q\) do not interfere, so the changes in \(y\) add. A deep network has far more paths than this one. Stack ten diamonds and the graph has \(2^{10} = 1{,}024\) paths from the first node to the last. Backpropagation never lists them. At a node it adds up the slopes that have arrived and sends one number on. Its cost grows with the number of edges and not with the number of paths.

The shark network

The shark network has the same structure. The input \(x_1\) feeds both \(z_1\) and \(z_2\), so \(\partial L/\partial x_1\) has two terms (steps 8 and 11 of the figure in “Sending the slopes back”). With the starting weights the slopes arriving at \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) are \(-0.579\) and \(+0.516\):

−0.463path through z1 (−0.579 × 0.8)+−0.206path through z2 (0.516 × −0.4)=−0.670∂L/∂x1

For \(x_2\) the two paths are \(+0.347\) and \(+0.361\), which total \(+0.709\). For \(x_1\) the paths have the same sign and add up. When they have opposite signs they partly cancel, so an input can have a large effect along both paths and a small effect in total.

A weight used at several places

The same rule covers a weight that is used more than once. The filters of a convolutional network (C1) slide over a picture, so one weight reads many positions. Take a weight \(w = 2\) that multiplies three values \(a = (1.0, 2.0, 0.5)\), so the score is \(o = wa_1 + wa_2 + wa_3\). Suppose the slope arriving at \(o\) is \(-0.4\). The use at \(a_k\) adds \(-0.4\,a_k\), which gives \(-0.4\), \(-0.8\) and \(-0.2\). The slope of \(w\) is their sum.

−0.4use at a1 = 1.0+−0.8use at a2 = 2.0+−0.2use at a3 = 0.5=−1.4∂L/∂w

Gradient accumulation in PyTorch

In code, a library adds a new contribution into the slope it has stored for a node. That is why PyTorch asks you to clear the stored slopes with zero_grad() before the next batch (0.1). Used on purpose, the same addition is called gradient accumulation. To imitate a batch that does not fit in memory, people run, for example, 4 to 16 smaller batches and call backward() on all of them before one optimiser step. Divide the loss of a small batch by the number of small batches, so that the sum matches the average of the big one.

The block below uses the weight shared at three places. The second call of backward() adds a second \(-1.4\) to the stored slope, and clearing the slope resets it. zero_grad() does this for all the weights (current PyTorch sets the stored slope to None by default, which has the same effect).

import torch

w = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=True)       # one weight, used at three places
a = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0, 0.5])
for call in (1, 2):
    o = (w * a).sum()                           # o = w a1 + w a2 + w a3
    (-0.4 * o).backward()                       # the slope arriving at o is -0.4
    print("after backward call", call, ": w.grad =", round(w.grad.item(), 4))
w.grad.zero_()                                  # clear the slope; optimizer.zero_grad() clears all weights
print("after zero_grad: w.grad =", w.grad.item())
after backward call 1 : w.grad = -1.4
after backward call 2 : w.grad = -2.8
after zero_grad: w.grad = 0.0

Common mistakes

Debug tip. A classic bug in hand-written backward code is writing = where += belongs for a node with two children. The result looks plausible, because it contains one of the two paths. The gradient check at the end of this chapter finds it.

More questions

You call loss.backward() on two batches in a row and then take one optimiser step, without clearing the stored slopes in between. What slope does the step use?

The sum of the two batch slopes, which is about twice the slope of one batch, so the step is about twice as long. Clearing the stored slopes before a new batch (zero_grad()) prevents this.

Whole layers at once

Guess first. A layer takes three inputs \(\mathbf{h} = (1.0,\, 2.0,\, 0.0)\) and has two neurons. The slopes arriving at the neurons are \(\boldsymbol\delta = (-0.5,\, 0.2)\). How many numbers does the slope of the weight matrix \(W\) have, and what is its entry for neuron 1 and input 2?

A layer computes one score per neuron, \(\mathbf{z} = W\mathbf{h} + \mathbf{b}\), with the biases in \(\mathbf{b}\). The weight matrix \(W\) is a table of numbers with one row per neuron and one column per input. Entry \(i\) of \(W\mathbf{h}\) adds the products of the weights in row \(i\) with the inputs. Here \(\boldsymbol\delta\) (delta) is the slope of the loss with respect to \(\mathbf{z}\), one number per neuron. The rules of the last two sections give the slope of \(W\) as the outer product of \(\boldsymbol\delta\) and \(\mathbf{h}\), the table of all products \(\delta_i h_j\). The slope sent to the inputs is \(W^\top\boldsymbol\delta\), where the transpose \(W^\top\) is \(W\) with rows and columns swapped.

  1. Drag the sliders for \(\delta_1\), \(\delta_2\), \(h_1\), \(h_2\) and \(h_3\). The table \(\partial L/\partial W\) has a row per neuron and a column per input, and its entry in row \(i\) and column \(j\) follows \(\delta_i h_j\).
  2. Drag \(h_3\) from 0 to 1: the third column changes from zeros to \(-0.5\) and \(0.2\).
  3. Choose Three sharks, averaged: a batch is a group of examples, and the new table is the average of the tables of three sharks. The last row still shows \(W^\top\boldsymbol\delta\) for shark 1 only. Then choose One shark and set \(\boldsymbol\delta = (-0.5, 0.2)\) and \(\mathbf{h} = (1.0, 2.0, 0.0)\).

The weight slope is a 2 by 3 table with six numbers, and its entry for neuron 1 and input 2 is \(-0.5 \times 2.0 = -1.0\).

How it works

Take the first setting of the figure, \(\boldsymbol\delta = (-0.5, 0.2)\) and \(\mathbf{h} = (1.0,\, 2.0,\, 0.0)\). The weight \(W_{ij}\) appears only in the score \(z_i = \sum_j W_{ij}h_j + b_i\), where it multiplies \(h_j\), so its local slope is \(h_j\) and its slope is \(\partial L/\partial W_{ij} = \delta_i h_j\). The input \(h_j\) is used by both neurons, so by the rule of the last section its slope is the sum \(\sum_i \delta_i W_{ij}\). That sum is the \(j\)th entry of \(W^\top\boldsymbol\delta\); for input 2 the figure's weights \(W_{12} = -0.3\) and \(W_{22} = 0.7\) give \((-0.3)(-0.5) + 0.7\times0.2 = 0.29\).

−0.5δ1×2.0h2=−1.0∂L/∂W12

The whole table is \(\begin{pmatrix}-0.5 & -1.0 & 0\\ 0.2 & 0.4 & 0\end{pmatrix}\), and \(W^\top\boldsymbol\delta = (-0.21, 0.29, -0.48)\) in the last row of the figure. The third column of the table is 0 because \(h_3 = 0\), and a large input would give its weights large slopes, which is one reason features are scaled.

Common belief. The slope that goes back through a layer uses the same matrix \(W\) as the forward pass.

Why it fails. Forward, \(W\) turns three inputs into two scores. Backward, two slopes must become three, which the 3 by 2 matrix \(W^\top\) does and the 2 by 3 matrix \(W\) cannot.

Better account. The backward pass uses \(W^\top\): the same numbers, read down the columns instead of along the rows.

Quick quiz

A layer has 100 inputs and 50 neurons. What are the sizes of \(W\), \(\boldsymbol\delta\) and the slope of \(W\)?

\(W\) is 50 by 100, \(\boldsymbol\delta\) has 50 entries and the slope of \(W\) is 50 by 100, the outer product of a 50-vector and a 100-vector. The slope sent to the inputs, \(W^\top\boldsymbol\delta\), has 100 entries.

Why does an input with the value 0 give its weights a slope of 0, whatever the arriving slope is?

The weight slope is \(\delta_i h_j\), and \(h_j = 0\) makes the product 0.

Go deeper worked batch, formulas for any layer, NumPy, PyTorch about 5 min

Layers in working models

The tiny network had one example and a few weights, so we could walk its graph node by node. Layers in a working model have hundreds or thousands of neurons, and the same three rules are applied to whole vectors. In code the batch average is one matrix product, \(\Delta^\top H\) divided by the batch size (0.5).

The tiny network in this form

Now the tiny network in this form, with the numbers of the first figure. Its output layer has \(\delta^{[2]} = p - y = -0.658\). The slope sent back to \(\mathbf{h}\) is \(W^{[2]\top}\delta^{[2]} = (0.9, -0.8) \times (-0.658) = (-0.592, 0.526)\). Multiplying entry by entry with the tanh slopes \((0.978, 0.980)\) gives \(\boldsymbol\delta^{[1]} = (-0.579, 0.516)\). Then \(\partial L/\partial W^{[1]}\) is the outer product of \(\boldsymbol\delta^{[1]}\) and \(\mathbf{x} = (0.22, 0.21)\). It is the 2 by 2 table \(\begin{pmatrix} -0.127 & -0.122\\ 0.114 & 0.108 \end{pmatrix}\), the same four slopes the graph found.

A batch with numbers

In the figure with three sharks, their arriving slopes are \(\boldsymbol\delta = (-0.5, 0.2)\), \((0.3, -0.4)\) and \((-0.2, 0.6)\), and their inputs are \((1.0, 2.0, 0.0)\), \((0.5, -1.0, 1.5)\) and \((1.5, 0.0, -0.5)\). For neuron 1 and input 2 the three products are \(-0.5\times2.0 = -1.0\), \(0.3\times(-1.0) = -0.3\) and \(-0.2\times0.0 = 0\). Their average is \(-0.433\). Doing this for all six entries together is one matrix product. Put the slopes of the sharks in the rows of \(\Delta\), the inputs in the rows of \(H\), and compute \(\Delta^\top H/3\).

import numpy as np

W = np.array([[0.5, -0.3, 0.8], [0.2, 0.7, -0.4]])                     # 2 neurons, 3 inputs
Delta = np.array([[-0.5, 0.2], [0.3, -0.4], [-0.2, 0.6]])               # one row of slopes per shark
H = np.array([[1.0, 2.0, 0.0], [0.5, -1.0, 1.5], [1.5, 0.0, -0.5]])     # one row of inputs per shark

print("shark 1, neuron 1, input 2:", Delta[0, 0] * H[0, 1])
dW = Delta.T @ H / len(H)               # the average of the three outer products
print("batch slope of W:", dW.round(3).tolist())
print("slope sent to the inputs, shark 1:", (W.T @ Delta[0]).round(2).tolist())
print("all three sharks at once:", (Delta @ W).round(2).tolist())
shark 1, neuron 1, input 2: -1.0
batch slope of W: [[-0.217, -0.433, 0.183], [0.3, 0.267, -0.3]]
slope sent to the inputs, shark 1: [-0.21, 0.29, -0.48]
all three sharks at once: [[-0.21, 0.29, -0.48], [0.07, -0.37, 0.4], [0.02, 0.48, -0.4]]

The slopes sent to the inputs are not averaged. A shark has its own values in the layer before this one, so its input slopes travel back separately. Only the weights and biases are shared by all sharks, so only their slopes are averaged. This is also why the memory of a backward pass grows with the batch size: the forward values of all sharks must be kept until their slopes come back.

With \(m\) examples, the slope of the average loss is the average of the per-example slopes, so \(\partial L/\partial W = \tfrac{1}{m}\Delta^\top H\). If you sum instead of averaging, all slopes are \(m\) times larger and the same \(\eta\) acts like a step \(m\) times bigger. Forgetting the \(1/m\) can be a reason why a network works at batch size 1 and diverges at batch size 64.

The formulas for any layer

\[ \boldsymbol\delta^{[l]} = \Big(W^{[l+1]\top}\boldsymbol\delta^{[l+1]}\Big)\odot g'\big(\mathbf{z}^{[l]}\big),\qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial W^{[l]}} = \boldsymbol\delta^{[l]}\,\mathbf{h}^{[l-1]\top},\qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{b}^{[l]}} = \boldsymbol\delta^{[l]} \]

  • \([l]\) is the layer number. \(\mathbf{h}^{[l-1]}\) is the layer's input, and \(\mathbf{h}^{[0]} = \mathbf{x}\).
  • \(\boldsymbol\delta^{[l]}\) is the slope of the loss with respect to \(\mathbf{z}^{[l]}\). The first formula sends it backward one layer: multiply by \(W^\top\), then by the activation's slope.
  • \(\odot\) multiplies two vectors entry by entry. \(g'\) is the slope of the activation, for example \(1 - \tanh^2 z\).
  • The slope of \(W\) is the outer product of \(\boldsymbol\delta^{[l]}\) and the input \(\mathbf{h}^{[l-1]}\); the slope of \(\mathbf{b}\) is \(\boldsymbol\delta^{[l]}\) itself.

The tiny network in NumPy

Here is the tiny network with arrays. The first block writes the forward pass and the backward pass by hand. It prints the same slopes that the graph showed.

import numpy as np

x = np.array([0.22, 0.21]); y = 1.0            # Tag 3305, scaled; label: adult
W1 = np.array([[0.8, -0.6], [-0.4, 0.7]]); b1 = np.array([0.1, -0.2])
W2 = np.array([0.9, -0.8]);                 b2 = -0.9

def forward(W1, b1, W2, b2):
    z1 = W1 @ x + b1;  h = np.tanh(z1)
    z2 = W2 @ h + b2;  p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z2))
    return z1, h, p, -np.log(p)                  # y = 1, so the loss is -ln p

z1, h, p, loss = forward(W1, b1, W2, b2)
d2 = p - y                      # slope at the output score
dW2, db2 = d2 * h, d2           # product node: the slope of W2 uses h
dh = d2 * W2                    # and the slope of h uses W2
d1 = dh * (1 - h ** 2)          # through tanh
dW1, db1 = np.outer(d1, x), d1  # outer product of slope and input

print("p =", round(p, 4), " loss =", round(loss, 4))
print("dW1 =", dW1.round(4).tolist())
print("db1 =", db1.round(4).tolist(), " dW2 =", dW2.round(4).tolist(), " db2 =", round(db2, 4))
p = 0.3421  loss = 1.0726
dW1 = [[-0.1274, -0.1216], [0.1135, 0.1084]]
db1 = [-0.579, 0.516]  dW2 = [-0.098, 0.0922]  db2 = -0.6579

The same in PyTorch

PyTorch builds the graph while the forward pass runs, and loss.backward() walks it backward. This is automatic differentiation: the library applies the rules of this chapter for you (0.1). The numbers match the hand-written version.

import numpy as np, torch

x = torch.tensor([0.22, 0.21], dtype=torch.float64); y = 1.0
W1 = torch.tensor([[0.8, -0.6], [-0.4, 0.7]], dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
b1 = torch.tensor([0.1, -0.2], dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
W2 = torch.tensor([0.9, -0.8], dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)
b2 = torch.tensor(-0.9, dtype=torch.float64, requires_grad=True)

h = torch.tanh(W1 @ x + b1)
p = torch.sigmoid(W2 @ h + b2)
loss = -torch.log(p)            # y = 1
loss.backward()                 # one backward pass fills all .grad

print("loss =", round(loss.item(), 4))
print("W1.grad =", W1.grad.numpy().round(4).tolist())
print("b1.grad =", b1.grad.numpy().round(4).tolist(), " W2.grad =", W2.grad.numpy().round(4).tolist(), " b2.grad =", round(b2.grad.item(), 4))
loss = 1.0726
W1.grad = [[-0.1274, -0.1216], [0.1135, 0.1084]]
b1.grad = [-0.579, 0.516]  W2.grad = [-0.098, 0.0922]  b2.grad = -0.6579

Common mistakes

Debug tip. The slope of an array must have the same size as the array. If dW1 comes out with a different size from W1, a transpose or an outer product is wrong. The update W1 -= eta * dW1 will then either fail or quietly broadcast. Print the sizes of all arrays once.

More questions

A batch of three sharks gives the slopes \(-1.0\), \(-0.3\) and \(0\) for one entry of \(W\). What is the slope of the average loss, and what happens if you add them and forget to divide by 3?

The average is \(-1.3/3 = -0.433\). The sum \(-1.3\) is three times too large, so the step acts as if \(\eta\) were three times bigger. A rate that was stable at batch size 1 may then diverge.

Long chains of small slopes

Guess first. Take a chain of 12 layers, one sigmoid neuron in a layer, with all weights equal to 1. The output layer starts with a slope of 1. About how much slope reaches layer 1: close to 1, about 0.01, or less than 0.0000001?

In the chain, layer \(j\) has the score \(z_j = w\,h_{j-1}\) and the value \(h_j = g(z_j)\), for a weight \(w\) and an activation \(g\). Going back one layer multiplies the arriving slope by \(w\,g'(z)\), where \(g'\) is the slope of the activation. The slope \(s_k\) that reaches layer \(k\) is then a product with one factor per layer in between. An extra layer multiplies it by one more factor, so it shrinks exponentially with depth when the factors are below 1. This is a vanishing gradient (the gradient is the set of slopes of the weights): with plain gradient descent the early layers barely learn. Factors above 1 make it grow, which is an exploding gradient.

  1. Start with sigmoid units, weight 1: the bars (log axis, so a gridline is ten times the one below) fall towards layer 1, and the box under the plot reports a slope of \(7.5\times10^{-8}\) at layer 1.
  2. Choose ReLU and drag Weight to 1.2: the bars grow towards layer 1, which receives 7.4. At weight 0.8 they shrink and layer 1 receives 0.086.
  3. Choose tanh and set Weight to 1: layer 1 receives 0.24, and at 1.5 it receives \(1.0\times10^{-4}\). Then choose sigmoid and set Weight to 1.

With sigmoid units and weights of 1, the factor per layer is about 0.22, so layer 1 receives less than a ten-millionth of the output layer's slope.

How it works

Take the figure's sigmoid chain. The sigmoid's slope is \(g' = h(1-h)\), at most 0.25. The chain starts from the input \(h_0 = 0.5\), so in layer 2 \(h_2 = 0.651\) and \(g' = 0.227\). With \(w = 1\) the factor is \(f = w\,g' = 0.227\). A chain of 12 layers has 11 factors between the output and layer 1, so \(s_1 = f^{11} \approx 8\times10^{-8}\). The figure shows \(7.5\times10^{-8}\) because the factor varies slightly between layers.

w = 1weight×0.227g′ in layer 2=0.227factor f per layer→ 11 factors →f11 ≈ 8×10−8slope s1 at layer 1

ReLU, \(\max(0, z)\), has slope 1 while its score is above 0, so its factor is \(w\). A weight below 1 makes the slope vanish over many layers. A weight above 1 makes it grow: with \(w = 1.2\), \(1.2^{11} = 7.4\) at 12 layers and \(1.2^{29} \approx 198\) at 30 layers. Tanh has slope 1 at a score of 0 and less elsewhere, so its factors stay near 1 only for small scores. A saturated unit has a score in a flat tail of the activation (the slope rules), where \(g'\) is near 0. Its factor is small unless \(w\) is very large.

Analogy. A message whispered down a line of people, where a person repeats it at 22% of the volume they heard. A person who repeats it louder is a factor above 1, the exploding case.

Where it breaks. A line has one path, but a layer mixes many inputs, so some paths can stay strong while others fade.

Quick quiz

Weights are 1 and the activation is ReLU with scores above 0. What is the factor per layer?

\(1 \times 1 = 1\): the weight times the ReLU slope. The slope neither vanishes nor explodes, until a score falls to 0 or below and the ReLU slope becomes 0.

With sigmoids and weights of 1, about how many layers back from the output does the slope fall below one in a million?

The factor is about 0.22. Nine factors give \(0.22^{9} \approx 1.2\times10^{-6}\), which is still above one in a million, and ten factors give \(0.22^{10} \approx 2.7\times10^{-7}\). Ten factors mean ten layers back, which is layer 2 of the 12-layer chain.

Go deeper product formula, ReLU example, worked chain, code about 5 min

Terms

With a vanishing gradient the early layers barely change in a step. With an exploding gradient one step throws the early weights far away. A unit is saturated when it is stuck in a flat tail of its activation, where its slope is close to 0 (0.6).

The product in symbols

The slope that arrives at layer \(k\) is \(s_k = \partial h_N/\partial h_k\). The chain rule gives \(s_k = s_{k+1}\cdot w\,g'(z_{k+1})\), and \(s_N = 1\), so \(s_k = \prod_{j=k+1}^{N} w\,g'(z_j)\). If the factor \(f = w\,g'\) were the same in all layers, then \(s_1 = f^{N-1}\). With \(f = 0.227\) and \(N = 12\), \(0.227^{11} \approx 8\times10^{-8}\).

\[ s_k = \prod_{j=k+1}^{N} w\,g'(z_j) \qquad s_1 = f^{\,N-1}\ \text{when the factor } f = w\,g' \text{ is the same in all layers} \]

  • \(s_k\) is the slope that arrives at layer \(k\), starting from \(s_N = 1\) at the output. \(w\) is the weight of the chain and \(g'(z_j)\) the slope of the activation in layer \(j\).
  • A factor below 1 shrinks the slope exponentially with depth, and a factor above 1 grows it. The sigmoid's slope is at most 0.25, so with \(w = 1\) the factor is at most 0.25.

A second example: ReLU and 30 layers

f = 1.2factor, ReLU on→ 30 layers →1.229 ≈ 198slope at layer 1 (explodes)|f = 0.8factor→ 30 layers →0.829 ≈ 0.0015slope at layer 1 (vanishes)

This second example uses ReLU and 30 layers and shows how thin the balance is. A weight of 1.2 makes the slope 198 times larger at layer 1. A weight of 0.8 makes it about 0.0015 times as large. A change of 20% in either direction pushes the chain out of balance.

A worked chain with three different scores

A sigmoid neuron whose score is \(z\) has slope \(\sigma(z)\,(1-\sigma(z))\), at most 0.25 at \(z = 0\). Take three layers whose scores are \(0.5\), \(-1\) and \(2\). Their slopes are 0.235, 0.197 and 0.105. With weights of 1 the arriving slope is multiplied by all three.

slope left0.235score 0.5×0.197score −1×0.105score 2=0.0049slope left after three layers

Already after three layers the slope is down by a factor of 200. The layer with score 2 is close to the flat tail, where the slope is small. A larger weight does not repair this. A weight of 4 gives a factor \(4\times0.25 = 1\) at a score of 0. It also makes the scores larger (\(z = 4h\)) and pushes the units toward the tails. Set the weight to 4 with sigmoids in the figure. The slope reaching layer 1 of the 12-layer chain falls from \(7.5\times10^{-8}\) to \(7.6\times10^{-13}\).

The activation matters as much as the weight

With weights of 1, the slope reaching layer 1 of the 12-layer chain is 24% of the starting slope with tanh, because the scores are small and tanh has slopes between 0.81 and 0.92 there. Raise the weight to 1.5 and the slope reaching layer 1 is only \(10^{-4}\) of it, because the scores grow towards 1.3, where the slope of tanh has fallen to 0.26 and the factor to \(1.5\times0.26 = 0.39\). With ReLU all of the slope arrives while the units are on. The code reproduces these numbers.

import numpy as np

def slope_at_layer_1(act, w, n=12, a0=0.5):
    h, factors = a0, []
    for k in range(n):
        z = w * h
        if act == "sigmoid":  h = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z)); local = h * (1 - h)
        elif act == "tanh":   h = np.tanh(z);           local = 1 - h ** 2
        else:                 h = max(0.0, z);          local = 1.0 if z > 0 else 0.0
        factors.append(w * local)
    return np.prod(factors[1:])              # one factor per layer after the first

for act, w in [("sigmoid", 1), ("sigmoid", 4), ("tanh", 1), ("tanh", 1.5), ("relu", 1), ("relu", 1.2), ("relu", 0.8)]:
    print(f"{act:8s} weight {w}: slope reaching layer 1 = {slope_at_layer_1(act, w):.1e}")
sigmoid  weight 1: slope reaching layer 1 = 7.5e-08
sigmoid  weight 4: slope reaching layer 1 = 7.6e-13
tanh     weight 1: slope reaching layer 1 = 2.4e-01
tanh     weight 1.5: slope reaching layer 1 = 1.0e-04
relu     weight 1: slope reaching layer 1 = 1.0e+00
relu     weight 1.2: slope reaching layer 1 = 7.4e+00
relu     weight 0.8: slope reaching layer 1 = 8.6e-02

Where this picture is too simple

A layer in a working network has many units, and its factor is the size of a whole matrix times the activation slopes. What matters is how much that matrix stretches the slope vector on average. Some directions can shrink while others grow, so a deep network is rougher than a clean power of one number. In practice, a deep sigmoid network often trains badly with plain random weights, and the trouble grows with depth. Exploding slopes show up as a loss that jumps to a huge value or to NaN. The usual remedies are a better weight scale and normalisation (B6) and, for explosions, a clip on the size of the slope (B8). A common mistake is to swap sigmoid for ReLU and assume the problem is gone. ReLU gives a slope of 1 only while the unit is on, and a unit that is off passes no slope back.

This chapter only shows the arithmetic. B6 measures it layer by layer in a deep network and shows the three fixes: a good starting scale for the weights, normalisation layers and residual connections. B8 shows how to detect the problem by printing gradient sizes per layer.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. If the weights of the first layers barely change while the last layers' weights move much more, print the size of the slope per layer. A drop of a factor of 10 per layer is a vanishing gradient.

Where this is used

Used in: B6 (initialisation, normalisation, residual connections) and B8 (gradient norms per layer, clipping).

More questions

A sigmoid chain has weights of 4, so the factor is 1 at a score of 0. Why does the slope still vanish?

The weight of 4 makes the scores large. A unit with score 2 has slope 0.105, so its factor is \(4\times0.105 = 0.42\). Units nearer the tails give smaller factors still, and the 12-layer chain delivers about \(10^{-12}\) of the slope to layer 1.

Gradient checking

Guess first. You can test a slope by nudging a weight up and down by a small \(h\), running the network at both nudges, and comparing the two losses. Which \(h\) gives the best estimate: 0.1, 0.00001 or \(10^{-15}\)? And how many extra runs of the network does the test need for the nine weights and biases?

Gradient checking compares the slopes from backpropagation with finite differences, which estimate a slope from two nearby points instead of a formula. The central difference \((L(w+h)-L(w-h))/2h\) uses the losses at \(w+h\) and \(w-h\). The relative error \(|a-b|/(|a|+|b|)\), where \(|x|\) is \(x\) without its sign, compares two slopes \(a\) and \(b\) without depending on their units. A nudge \(h\) that is too large and one that is too small both give a wrong slope, so the best size lies in between.

  1. Drag the nudge size \(h\) from \(10^0\) down to \(10^{-15}\) and follow the coral dot on the central curve (for \(w_{11}\)). The error falls to about \(10^{-11}\) near \(h = 10^{-5}\) and rises again for smaller \(h\).
  2. Choose a bug, such as wrong sign on \(p - y\): the status line reports an error near 1 whatever \(h\) is.
  3. Read the cost line under the table: the central check runs the network 18 times, and backpropagation needs one forward pass and one backward pass.

parameterbackpropnudgingrelative errorverdict

The central-difference error falls to about \(10^{-11}\) near \(h = 10^{-5}\) and rises again on both sides, while a bug keeps it large for all \(h\).

How it works

Take \(w_{11} = 0.8\) and \(h = 0.01\). Running the network with \(w_{11} = 0.81\) gives \(L = 1.0713761\), and with \(w_{11} = 0.79\) it gives \(L = 1.0739237\). The central difference is \((1.0713761 - 1.0739237)/0.02 = -0.12738\), and backpropagation gave \(-0.12738\) too.

L = 1.0713761at w + h−L = 1.0739237at w − h=−0.0025476difference÷0.022h=−0.12738central estimatevs−0.12738backprop

The one-sided estimate \((L(w+h)-L(w))/h = -0.1273\) is off in the fourth digit because the loss curve bends. Its error grows in proportion to \(h\), and the central error grows like \(h^2\) (the Go deeper section shows why). The figure labels a relative error below \(10^{-7}\) “great”, below \(10^{-5}\) “fine”, below \(10^{-3}\) “look closer” and above that “wrong”. These cut-offs are conventions, and other sources use other ones. The three bugs of the figure keep the error for all nine slopes together between 0.008 and 1.0, for any \(h\) from 0.01 down to \(10^{-12}\).

Common belief. A slope is the limit as \(h\) goes to 0, so the smaller the \(h\), the better the estimate.

Why it fails. A computer keeps about 16 digits in float64, the 64-bit format that NumPy uses by default. With \(h = 10^{-15}\) the losses \(L(w+h)\) and \(L(w-h)\) are equal in nearly all of them, so their difference is mostly rounding noise.

Better account. Use an \(h\) near \(10^{-5}\) with the central difference in float64. Float32 keeps about 7 digits, so its best \(h\) is much larger, which is why checks run in float64.

Quick quiz

The backprop slope is −0.1274 and the one-sided nudge estimate is −0.1273. Is the code probably right?

The relative error is \(0.0001/0.2547 \approx 4\times10^{-4}\), in the figure's “look closer” band. A one-sided estimate is off in the fourth digit because the loss curve bends, so run the central difference before you blame the code. A correct backward pass reaches \(10^{-7}\) or better at a good \(h\) with the central difference.

Why does the central difference need two runs per weight, and is that worth it?

It evaluates the loss at \(w + h\) and \(w - h\). Its error shrinks like \(h^2\) instead of \(h\), so it reaches a much lower error at the same \(h\). That is worth the extra run in a test you only run once.

Go deeper Taylor argument, round-off, practice, Python, float32 about 7 min

More slopes by hand

The same test on an output weight, \(v_1 = 0.9\), with \(h = 0.01\): \(L(0.91) = 1.071670\) and \(L(0.89) = 1.073629\). The difference is \(-0.001959\), and dividing by 0.02 gives \(-0.09795\). Backprop gave \(-0.09795\) as well (\(-0.0980\) to three digits in the last section). A bias works the same way. For \(c\), the losses 1.066081 at \(-0.89\) and 1.079239 at \(-0.91\) give \(-0.6579\), and backprop gave \(-0.6579\).

Why the central difference is more accurate

The one-sided estimate at the same \(h\) is \((1.0713761 - 1.0726491)/0.01 = -0.1273\), off in the fourth digit, and the central estimate agrees to six digits. To see why, write the loss near \(w\) as a polynomial in \(h\), the Taylor series:

\[ L(w \pm h) = L \pm h\,L_1 + \tfrac12 h^2 L_2 \pm \tfrac16 h^3 L_3 + \dots \]

  • Here \(L_1\) is the slope \(\partial L/\partial w\), \(L_2\) the curvature and \(L_3\) the next derivative of the loss along this one weight, all taken at \(w\).
  • Subtract \(L\) and divide by \(h\): the forward estimate is \(L_1 + \tfrac12 hL_2 + \dots\), so its error is about \(\tfrac12 hL_2\).
  • Subtract the two lines and divide by \(2h\): the even terms cancel and the central estimate is \(L_1 + \tfrac16 h^2 L_3 + \dots\), so its error is about \(\tfrac16 h^2 L_3\).

Round-off and the best h

Round-off adds a second error. A computer stores a number with a relative accuracy of about \(\varepsilon \approx 2\times10^{-16}\) in float64. A computed loss is off by about \(\varepsilon L\), so the difference divided by \(2h\) is off by about \(\varepsilon L/h\). The total error is about \(\tfrac16 h^2 L_3 + \varepsilon L/h\). It is smallest when \(h\) is near \(\varepsilon^{1/3} \approx 6\times10^{-6}\), up to the sizes of \(L\) and \(L_3\). That matches the dip of the curve in the figure. In float32 (\(\varepsilon \approx 10^{-7}\)) the best \(h\) is near 0.005 and the best relative error is about \(10^{-5}\), five digits against eleven in float64. That is why checks are done in float64.

Using the figure

The check uses the network of the figure in “Sending the slopes back”, with its current weights (change them there). For a large \(h\), the loss curve bends between \(w - h\) and \(w + h\), and the straight line through the two points no longer matches the slope. For a tiny \(h\), the two losses agree in their first 15 or so digits, and the computer keeps only about 16, so subtracting them leaves noise. The central difference beats the one-sided version at the same \(h\) because its bending error cancels to first order.

With a bug switched on, the error for all nine slopes together jumps to 0.008 or more and stays there however you move \(h\). That is the signal gradient checking gives: correct slopes agree to many digits at a good \(h\), while a wrong formula disagrees at the first or second digit.

In practice

For a large model you do not check all weights. Pick a few random weights from the layers and compare those. Use relative error, not the plain gap, because slopes in different layers have very different sizes. Typical readings in float64 are \(10^{-8}\) to \(10^{-11}\) for correct code and \(10^{-3}\) or more for a wrong formula (the three bugs of the figure give 0.008 to 1.0). Common mistakes are running the check in float32, leaving dropout on so that the loss changes between runs, and checking after an optimiser step instead of at the same weights.

Compare whole vectors with the norm formula below, and not one entry at a time. A weight with a true slope of \(10^{-12}\) has a relative error near 1 from rounding alone, and it should not fail the test. Remember also what the check tests. It compares the backward code with the forward code. If the forward code is wrong, for example a loss that uses the wrong label, the two agree and both are wrong. Look at the first loss and a few predictions as well (B8).

The check is far too slow for training. It needs two runs of the whole network per weight, so GPT-2 Small (124 million weights) would need about 248 million runs for one step. Backpropagation needs one forward pass and one backward pass, whatever the number of weights. Use the check once, on a small network and one example, whenever you write new backward code.

PyTorch's gradcheck expects double inputs and uses a nudge of \(10^{-6}\) by default.

The formulas in symbols

\[ \frac{L(w+h)-L(w)}{h}\;\;\text{(forward)}\qquad \frac{L(w+h)-L(w-h)}{2h}\;\;\text{(central)}\qquad \text{error} = \frac{\lVert \mathbf{a}-\mathbf{b}\rVert}{\lVert \mathbf{a}\rVert + \lVert \mathbf{b}\rVert} \]

  • \(h\) is the nudge and \(L(w+h)\) the loss with that one weight raised by \(h\). The first two formulas are estimates of \(\partial L/\partial w\).
  • The forward estimate is off by an amount that grows in proportion to \(h\); the central estimate is off by an amount that grows like \(h^2\). Round-off adds an error that grows like \(1/h\).
  • \(\mathbf{a}\) is the vector of backprop slopes and \(\mathbf{b}\) the vector of nudge estimates. Rules of thumb vary. For smooth networks in float64, an error near \(10^{-7}\) or below is a good sign, and an error of \(10^{-3}\) or more points to a bug.

Common mistakes

Debug tip. Check one small network and one example. Switch off dropout and any random augmentation (the loss must be the same on a second run), and use float64. A ReLU unit whose score is within \(h\) of 0 can make the check disagree even when the code is right, because the nudge crosses the corner.

In Python

import numpy as np

x = np.array([0.22, 0.21])
theta = np.array([0.8, -0.6, -0.4, 0.7, 0.1, -0.2, 0.9, -0.8, -0.9])   # W1 (4), b1 (2), W2 (2), b2

def loss_and_grad(t):
    W1, b1, W2, b2 = t[:4].reshape(2, 2), t[4:6], t[6:8], t[8]
    h = np.tanh(W1 @ x + b1)
    p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(W2 @ h + b2)))
    d2 = p - 1.0
    d1 = d2 * W2 * (1 - h ** 2)
    return -np.log(p), np.concatenate([np.outer(d1, x).ravel(), d1, d2 * h, [d2]])

_, g = loss_and_grad(theta)
for h in [1e-1, 1e-3, 1e-5, 1e-8, 1e-12, 1e-15]:
    est = np.zeros(9)
    for i in range(9):
        up, dn = theta.copy(), theta.copy()
        up[i] += h; dn[i] -= h
        est[i] = (loss_and_grad(up)[0] - loss_and_grad(dn)[0]) / (2 * h)
    err = np.linalg.norm(g - est) / (np.linalg.norm(g) + np.linalg.norm(est))
    print(f"h = {h:.0e}  relative error = {err:.1e}")
h = 1e-01  relative error = 1.0e-03
h = 1e-03  relative error = 1.0e-07
h = 1e-05  relative error = 8.2e-12
h = 1e-08  relative error = 9.0e-09
h = 1e-12  relative error = 1.1e-04
h = 1e-15  relative error = 1.1e-01

The same check in float32 shows the difference. The float64 rows are there for comparison. In float32 the error is smallest, about \(10^{-5}\), for \(h\) between 0.005 and 0.01, and it grows as \(h\) shrinks. At \(h = 10^{-5}\) it is \(4.8\times10^{-3}\), above the \(10^{-3}\) line that points to a bug, although the backward pass is correct.

import numpy as np

theta = np.array([0.8, -0.6, -0.4, 0.7, 0.1, -0.2, 0.9, -0.8, -0.9])

def make(dtype):                                  # the same network, in float32 or float64
    x = np.array([0.22, 0.21], dtype=dtype)
    def loss_and_grad(t):
        t = t.astype(dtype)
        W1, b1, W2, b2 = t[:4].reshape(2, 2), t[4:6], t[6:8], t[8]
        h = np.tanh(W1 @ x + b1)
        p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(W2 @ h + b2)))
        d2 = p - 1.0
        d1 = d2 * W2 * (1 - h ** 2)
        return -np.log(p), np.concatenate([np.outer(d1, x).ravel(), d1, d2 * h, [d2]])
    return loss_and_grad

for dtype in (np.float64, np.float32):
    f = make(dtype); _, g = f(theta)
    for h in (1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-5):
        est = np.zeros(9)
        for i in range(9):
            up, dn = theta.copy(), theta.copy()
            up[i] += h; dn[i] -= h
            est[i] = (f(up)[0] - f(dn)[0]) / (2 * h)
        err = np.linalg.norm(g - est) / (np.linalg.norm(g) + np.linalg.norm(est))
        print(f"{dtype.__name__}  h = {h:.0e}  relative error = {err:.1e}")
float64  h = 1e-02  relative error = 1.0e-05
float64  h = 1e-03  relative error = 1.0e-07
float64  h = 1e-05  relative error = 8.2e-12
float32  h = 1e-02  relative error = 1.4e-05
float32  h = 1e-03  relative error = 5.1e-05
float32  h = 1e-05  relative error = 4.8e-03

Where this is used

Used in: any new layer or loss you write by hand (this is the first test to run), and B8, where unit tests check one component at a time.

More questions

You check 5 randomly chosen weights of GPT-2 Small with the central difference. How many runs of the network is that, and how does it compare with checking all weights?

The check takes two runs per weight, so 10 runs, against about 248 million for all 124 million weights. A random sample can catch a wrong formula that affects all the weights of a layer, which is the usual case. A bug that touches only a few weights can slip through.

Exercises

Theory

  1. theory A node computes \(s = u\,v + u\). At \(u = 2\), \(v = 3\), find \(\partial s/\partial u\) and \(\partial s/\partial v\). If the slope arriving at \(s\) is 5, what slope reaches \(u\) and what slope reaches \(v\)? Why does \(u\) get contributions from two places?

    Hint

    Write the two terms of \(s\) separately and give \(u\) a slope from both.

  2. theory Show that for a sigmoid output \(p = \sigma(z_o)\) and log loss, the slope \(\partial\ell/\partial z_o\) equals \(p - y\) both for \(y = 1\) and for \(y = 0\). Evaluate it for the starting network (\(p = 0.342\)) with either label.

    Hint

    For \(y=1\): \(\ell = -\ln p\), so \(\partial\ell/\partial p = -1/p\). Multiply by \(p(1-p)\). For \(y=0\), \(\ell = -\ln(1-p)\).

  3. theory One run of a network takes 50 ms. How long does a central-difference check of all the weights take for the nine-weight network, and for GPT-2 Small with 124 million weights? Compare with backprop, which costs about three runs in total.

  4. theory In a chain of sigmoid layers with weights 1, a layer multiplies the slope by at most 0.25. How many layers can the slope cross before it is below \(10^{-6}\) in the best case? Why does the slope usually fall below that level sooner?

Practice

  1. practice Load the 268 spadenose records from the made-up catch table. Standardise length and girth, and train the two-layer tanh network of this chapter (two hidden units, label: mature) by full-batch gradient descent with your own NumPy backprop. Report the log loss and accuracy after 2,000 steps with \(\eta = 0.5\), and compare with the logistic regression of A3 (log loss 0.2318).

  2. practice Take the gradient-check code above and break the backward pass on purpose in three different ways. Drop the tanh slope, flip a sign, and pick one more yourself. For any bug, print the relative error per parameter and say which parameters the check blames.

  3. practice Rebuild the network in PyTorch in float64 and train it for 20 steps with torch.optim.SGD. Check that the weights after the first step agree with your NumPy update to 10 decimals.

Think deeper

  1. open Your gradient check passes on a tiny network at random weights, but training the big network diverges. List three reasons the check can pass while training fails, and say how you would test it.

  2. open The backward pass needs the forward values, so a very deep network must keep all of them in memory. Suggest ways to trade memory for extra computation, and say when it would be worth it.

  3. open At the starting weights, the slope of the loss with respect to the two inputs is about \(-0.67\) and \(+0.71\). A reader says "so a longer shark looks less adult to this network and a wider one more adult". What would you check before trusting that sentence? (B9 returns to input slopes.)

Come back later

Try these after two days and again after a week, before you open the answers.

Log loss with a sigmoid output has slope \(p - y\) at the score (A3). A shark is an adult, \(y = 1\), and the network says \(p = 0.9\). What is the slope, and what does its sign say about the score?

\(0.9 - 1 = -0.1\). A negative slope means that raising the score lowers the loss, so the update pushes the score up, but gently because \(p\) is already close to 1.

A weight's slope is \(\delta_i h_j\). Why did A2 rescale the length column before gradient descent, and how does this chapter's formula show the problem?

A column in centimetres has large values, so the weight attached to it gets slopes that are large compared with the slopes of the bias. The valley of the loss becomes long and narrow, and one learning rate suits neither direction. Standardised columns make the slopes comparable.

The local slopes along a chain are 3, 0.5 and 0.1 (0.6). What slope arrives at the start? What if the last local slope were a ReLU's 0?

\(3 \times 0.5 \times 0.1 = 0.15\). With a 0 anywhere in the chain the product is 0, so no slope arrives and the weights upstream get none at all.
